extracted.intended_audience: college mathematics instructors (tenure-track faculty, teaching professors, instructors, adjuncts, graduate TAs, undergraduate learning assistants) and others teaching mathematics
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for college-level mathematics instructors on designing and implementing classroom practices that disrupt hierarchies and promote equitable student participation, grounded in research and equity-analytics data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concrete teaching practices over abstract theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Focus on concrete teaching practices that you can implement today, alongside supporting explanations of the theory and evidence behind those practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start with actionable techniques and brief theoretical summaries; provide examples of what implementation looks like. The book emphasizes readability and practical usefulness for instructors with little formal training in education.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instruction, practice, and feedback as the three core ingredients
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective teaching consists of instruction, practice, and feedback; all three are necessary components of learning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely primarily on lecture (instruction); prioritize creating learning environments that promote effective practice and provide meaningful feedback. Treat lecture as a small ingredient rather than the default model.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use data with social marker specificity (equity analytics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use data that can speak to the experiences of social marker groups (e.g., women, students of color, Black women) so instructors can reflect and take up strategies to address inequities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid treating equitable teaching as one-size-fits-all; disaggregate participation/assessment data by relevant social markers (the EQUIP tool and equity analytics methodology are cited). Use data to surface specific patterns and inform targeted practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt incremental change with coaching and community support
rubrics_metrics.description: Change is most effective when incremental: instructors adopt one new practice at a time and watch its impact on data, ideally with coaching or a supportive community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide regular feedback (e.g., classroom participation data), use coaching (one-on-one or community-based), and iterate across a year or more. Even solo readers can use peer observation or video to generate feedback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Move from instructor-centered to student-centered, interactive instruction
rubrics_metrics.description: Shift classrooms away from 'pure lecture' toward more interactive formats (e.g., interactive lecture, think–pair–share, small-group work) so students can practice and engage socially.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you currently lecture exclusively, start by explicitly building community early and incorporating questioning strategies, opportunities to work on parts of problems, and peer interactions. These shifts support more equitable participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manage participation intentionally to reduce domination
rubrics_metrics.description: Intentionally structure participation so that a small number of privileged students do not dominate discussions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid allowing shout-outs or calling on the first hand by default; adopt strategies that ensure everyone has a chance to share. Use data to detect predictable domination patterns (based on gender, race, disability) and adjust facilitation practices accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide meaningful feedback beyond grades
rubrics_metrics.description: Meaningful feedback (not just grades and a few comments) is essential to learning and improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate formative feedback mechanisms, peer critique, coaching, and targeted comments. Use assessment to foster both interdependence and independence, not merely summative grading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incorporate authentic, domain-specific practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Include authentic mathematical practices in class (e.g., making conjectures, proving theorems, modeling phenomena) and view practice both as repeated engagement and as domain activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design class activities that mirror authentic mathematical work and provide repeated opportunities for students to practice these activities with feedback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implementation fidelity matters for active-learning techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: Techniques labeled as 'active learning', 'flipped classroom', or 'inquiry-based' can be effective if implemented well; poor implementation can lead instructors to conclude incorrectly that the technique 'does not work.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop the necessary skills and practices to make a chosen technique effective; treat initial failures as a sign of implementation issues rather than disproof of the paradigm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use theory to inform design while recognizing limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Educational theories (e.g., status, identity, formative assessment, stereotype threat) provide concrete insights for instructional design, but broad paradigms alone do not specify optimal classroom actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine paradigms (constructivist, sociocultural) with specific theories and design research to translate theory into usable instructional interventions. Be cautious about claiming simple 'what works' answers from broad theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collect and analyze classroom participation data to reveal patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: Observe and code classroom participation to identify predictable patterns of hierarchy and domination based on axes like gender, race, and disability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use empirical data (e.g., EQUIP observations) to document participation disparities and to track the impact of implemented practices over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge systemic limits and treat equitable teaching as harm reduction
rubrics_metrics.description: Equitable teaching is important and necessary but is not a panacea; classroom practices cannot alone eliminate broader social oppression that bounds what can be accomplished.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be realistic about goals: use classroom change as a form of harm reduction and as part of broader efforts; situate teaching efforts within historical and societal contexts (e.g., white supremacy, patriarchy, ableism).

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt a teacher-as-coach model (organize practice and feedback)
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective teachers act as coaches who organize learning environments for practice and provide feedback, rather than relying primarily on performance/modeling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that teaching and high-level performance are distinct skills: prioritize designing effective practice and giving useful feedback rather than only demonstrating expertise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design learning with mediating artifacts and representations
rubrics_metrics.description: Use representational tools (notation, number-lines, symbols, language, physical artifacts) to mediate thinking and make complex mathematical ideas accessible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage mediators to develop students' conceptual understanding (e.g., counting with fingers, symbolic notation); consider how representations change cognition and support learning.
